title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation
authors: Zhuoyang Li, Teng Shi, Jiakai Tang, Weijie Yu, Guofu Xie, Xiao Zhang
abstract: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

infographic.key_insight: GainReason trains generative recommenders by rewarding reasoning sentences for how much they increase the target item's Semantic ID log-likelihood.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Sentence-level predictive rewards provide more discriminative training signals than rewards based only on final recommendation performance.
method: Measure Predictive Gain (PG) as the change in target Semantic ID log-likelihood induced by each reasoning sentence.
Optimize reasoning with PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO), using custom causal attention for efficient reward computation.
Add PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) to strengthen reasoning-conditioned prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent improvements over competitive baselines on three public benchmarks and theoretically establishes alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective.
infographic.watch_item: Custom causal attention adds implementation complexity, and the abstract does not quantify training overhead or benchmark improvement magnitudes.
infographic.paper_title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation

title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
authors: Blas Eugenio Vicco Zarate, Miguel Hernán Vicco
abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires adaptation to changing conditions while preserving performance under previously encountered dynamics. It was investigated whether specialists generated by evolutionary search can provide a reusable memory when combined with environment detection and failure-driven search. The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them through Bayesian policy reuse. The architecture was evaluated in non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah environments. In the 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the complete architecture achieved a mean success rate of 83.2% across the five test environments. Among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments, the complete architecture showed the most consistent retention. A selection ablation also showed that the retrieval rule affected performance. In the evaluated sequences, ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and achieved lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah. The evidence concerns the complete architecture and does not isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.

infographic.key_insight: ENA combines evolved specialist policies with regime-indexed memory and Bayesian reuse to support adaptation while retaining performance under previously encountered dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Archiving and retrieving policies by detected dynamics offers a reusable-memory design for reinforcement-learning controllers operating under changing conditions.
method: Evolve small neural-network policies without gradients.
Archive specialists by detected dynamic regime and retrieve them through Bayesian policy reuse.
Trigger evolutionary search in response to failures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah, complete ENA averaged 83.2% success across five test environments in a 30-replicate CartPole ablation and showed the most consistent retention among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments.
infographic.watch_item: ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and earned lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah; the results neither isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention nor establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.
infographic.paper_title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent

title: When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents
authors: Zeynab Anbiaee, Sajjad Dadkhah, Ali A. Ghorbani
abstract: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly act as agents that select and invoke external tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes this interaction by allowing clients to compose tools advertised by multiple servers. However, tool metadata used for discovery and selection is not, by itself, necessarily bound to a verified provider identity. This paper studies this gap as tool-provider misbinding: a failure in which a request intended for a legitimate provider is instead resolved to an attacker-controlled tool. The attacker does not compromise the host, LLM, legitimate server, or network channel; it only operates another MCP server that advertises tools with chosen metadata. We formulate tool provider misbinding as an attacker-controlled tool-selection optimization problem and evaluate it in a controlled MCP environment across five LLM-based clients. The results show that interactions drive misbinding. The strongest failures occur when exact-name collision, task-aligned description, and compatible schema reinforce one another, but authority-enhanced descriptions with compatible schema can also cause wrong-provider execution or unresolved provider ambiguity without name collision. Different models expose the same provider-binding weakness differently, including attacker-controlled provider selection, clarification requests, and unstable or inconsistent provider resolution.

infographic.key_insight: In MCP-based AI agents, tool names and metadata do not necessarily establish provider identity, allowing attacker-advertised tools to receive requests intended for legitimate providers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: MCP integrations should bind tool discovery and invocation to verified provider identities rather than rely on names, descriptions, or schema compatibility.
method: Formulate tool-provider misbinding as an attacker-controlled tool-selection optimization problem.
Operate an attacker MCP server with chosen tool metadata, without compromising legitimate components or network channels.
Evaluate metadata interactions in a controlled MCP environment across five LLM-based clients.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five clients, the strongest failures combined exact-name collisions, task-aligned descriptions, and compatible schemas; authority-enhanced descriptions also induced wrong-provider execution or ambiguity without name collisions.
infographic.watch_item: The controlled evaluation shows client-dependent failure modes, but the abstract provides no quantitative misbinding rates or evidence of prevalence in deployed systems.
infographic.paper_title: When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents

title: Emergent Steering Beyond Endpoint Alignment in Chemical Reaction Models
authors: Yili Shen, Kehan Guo, Haomin Zhuang, Xiangliang Zhang
abstract: Machine learning models for chemical reaction prediction are usually evaluated by endpoint accuracy, but endpoint correctness alone does not reveal how a model represents chemical transformation or why it fails. We introduce UniRxnAxis, a unified forward-retrosynthesis framework that models both tasks as direction-conditioned endpoint redistribution in a shared latent space. By aligning source states, transformed states, and encoded target endpoints, UniRxnAxis enables directional auditing of learned latent updates. This shared latent geometry allows the learned displacement (from the encoder source state $S_0$ to the decoder-facing transformed state $S_1$) to be decomposed into an endpoint-parallel component and an endpoint-orthogonal residual, which we call emergent steering. Our evaluation shows that emergent steering is functionally important: in retrosynthesis, it recovers most of the model's utility, remains effective under random, shuffled, and prototype controls, and directly affects which bond edits are promoted or suppressed. The residual-over-parallel ordering persists across alignment strengths, after decoder-interface calibration, against angle-matched random axes, and in a second graph-edit architecture, although its magnitude depends on the reference axis and optimization. The decomposition also supports a proxy taxonomy of model-side failures, showing how reaction models can be audited beyond endpoint accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Chemical reaction models use endpoint-orthogonal latent updates—termed emergent steering—that contribute substantially to predictions beyond movement toward the encoded target.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Auditing latent update directions can reveal model failures and bond-edit behavior that endpoint accuracy alone misses.
method: Unify forward prediction and retrosynthesis as direction-conditioned endpoint redistribution in a shared latent space.
Decompose source-to-transformed latent updates into endpoint-parallel movement and an orthogonal steering residual.
Evaluate each component with controls, decoder-interface calibration, and a second graph-edit architecture.
infographic.evidence_signal: In retrosynthesis, steering recovers most model utility, affects promoted or suppressed bond edits, and outperforms the parallel component across multiple controls and evaluation settings.
infographic.watch_item: The measured steering magnitude depends on the reference axis and optimization, so the decomposition should not be treated as a unique chemical mechanism.
infographic.paper_title: Emergent Steering Beyond Endpoint Alignment in Chemical Reaction Models

title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection
authors: Yipeng Du, Yuxi Li, Ying Zhang, Chong Sun, Chen Li, Jing Lyu
abstract: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.

infographic.key_insight: WeVisForensics improves AI-generated video detection by jointly refining an investigator agent and forensic inspectors that ground verdicts in localized visual and audio evidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a design for adaptive forensic pipelines that select relevant inspections rather than relying on fixed workflows or single-pass reasoning.
method: An investigator selects artifact types, inspection windows, and when to conclude.
Specialized inspector agents examine visual and audio cues and return forensic evidence.
Dual-timescale policy optimization pairs fast investigator reinforcement learning with slower inspector refinement guided by annotated artifact intervals.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors introduce ForenCue-30K and report 95.2% average detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain, and agentic benchmarks, described as 9.0% above the strongest prior detector.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment latency, inspection costs, and robustness to future video generators are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection

title: ViRA: Toward Ultra-High-Resolution Visual Agents via Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization
authors: Huawei Lin, Jinting Liu, Tongyan Wang, Xuyang Chen, Ruihua Shi, Zhichao Xu
abstract: Visual agents answer questions about ultra-high-resolution photos by zooming into the relevant regions. However, existing agents often answer from common sense instead of reading the evidence. Reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer cannot correct this, because a guess earns the same reward as reading. We propose Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization (CrossRPO), which trains agents on contrast sets. A contrast set asks one question about several versions of an image that differ only in a small region with the evidence and have different answers, so only reading the evidence solves the whole set. CrossRPO rewards solving the whole set, and we prove that it does not reinforce a set answered from common sense. We build contrast sets for training (ViRA-Train) and evaluation (ViRA-Bench) by editing one small object in images of 21 to 120 megapixels, and we photograph further sets with real changes (ViRA-Bench-Real) to exclude editing traces. We train two Visual Reasoning Agents, ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B, with CrossRPO on only about 3,500 items of ViRA-Train each. CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at the maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO. ViRA-9B is the most accurate open model of its size on all benchmarks, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna, both at their highest thinking level, on most benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: CrossRPO rewards answering entire image contrast sets correctly, making evidence-based inspection more valuable than common-sense guessing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This training approach can improve visual agents that must zoom into small, decisive details in ultra-high-resolution images.
method: Create contrast sets sharing one question but differing in a small evidence region and its correct answer.
Use CrossRPO to reward solving the whole set rather than individual answers.
Train ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B on about 3,500 ViRA-Train items each.
infographic.evidence_signal: On ViRA-Bench at maximum resolution, CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy versus 59.3% for GRPO; evaluation also includes photographed real-change sets to check against editing traces.
infographic.watch_item: Constructing reliable contrast sets requires controlled, answer-changing image variations; performance beyond this benchmark setup remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: ViRA: Toward Ultra-High-Resolution Visual Agents via Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization

title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
authors: Bonam Mingole, Davis Yadav, Hui Min Lee, S. Shyam Sundar, Amulya Yadav
abstract: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

infographic.key_insight: Faculty-designed “AI-proof” college assessments remained vulnerable: the best-performing LLM scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them.
infographic.engineering_relevance: AI-resistant assessment design needs empirical testing rather than relying on question complexity or instructor intuition alone.
method: Collected 75 authentic college assessment questions across 17 disciplines, including 61 intentionally designed to resist LLMs.
Evaluated three state-of-the-art LLMs with and without supplementary course materials.
Identified five faculty design strategies through thematic analysis and tested their impact on answer accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The evaluation covered questions contributed by 37 faculty members from 11 U.S. and U.K. universities, alongside online-course questions, and found performance differences across models, answer formats, and design strategies.
infographic.watch_item: Results from 75 questions and three models may not generalize to all disciplines, assessment formats, or future LLMs.
infographic.paper_title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments

title: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems
authors: Nikolaos Kekatos, Georgios Koutidis, Konstantinos Antonakopoulos, Stylianos Basagiannis, Sokratis Katsikas, Georgios Kavallieratos
abstract: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. We instantiate it on two scenarios, a transmission operator under coordinated cyber compromise, sabotage and heatwave, and a distribution operator under a supply-chain compromise during a storm, and report an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies each pillar through false-data-injection attack detection, cyber-physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost.

infographic.key_insight: RESILAGENT proposes a three-pillar architecture that connects threat detection, simulation, decision-making and tamper-evident evidence for cyber-physical power-system resilience.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could help power-system operators coordinate responses to combined cyberattacks, physical sabotage and extreme weather rather than relying on siloed monitoring.
method: Organize operations into Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery.
Use a cloud orchestrator to coordinate agentic AI, multimodal models and real-time digital twins in a Detect–Simulate–Decide–Sign loop.
Anchor threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence on a permissioned blockchain.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes two operator threat scenarios and an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark covering false-data-injection detection, cyber-physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: As a concept architecture, operational reliability and safe AI-guided response under real-world latency, data-quality and infrastructure constraints remain to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems

title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning
authors: Yulun Wu, Nicola Bastianello, Karl Henrik Johansson, Matthieu Barreau
abstract: Modeling large multi-agent systems poses challenges for trajectory inference and parameter identification, as network size and coupling increase computational demands and partial observations require reconstructing unobserved states. We propose MAS-PINN, a neural-network architecture with a tailored training algorithm for a physics-informed learning framework that leverages the network topology and the agents' similarity to reduce computational and memory costs of simulating and identifying multi-agent systems. Its architecture represents agent trajectories through shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients. Training alternates between learning features, fitting coupled trajectories, and estimating physical parameters. A matrix-free update exploits local interactions to fit trajectories without forming large global matrices. Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka--Volterra networks, and Rössler oscillators show improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, including inference in large systems and identification under partial observations or unknown topology, alongside substantial computational savings in coefficient fitting.

infographic.key_insight: MAS-PINN uses shared temporal features and network structure to model coupled agents while reducing computational and memory costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could make simulation, trajectory reconstruction, and physical-parameter identification more practical for large, partially observed multi-agent systems.
method: Represent trajectories with shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients.
Alternate feature learning, coupled-trajectory fitting, and physical-parameter estimation.
Exploit local interactions through matrix-free coefficient updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka–Volterra networks, and Rössler oscillators report improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, plus substantial savings in coefficient fitting.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify speedups or establish performance on real-world systems beyond the tested dynamical models.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning

title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
authors: Arunkumar V, Manoranjan Gandhudi, Gangadharan G. R., Arun Prakash, S. Senthilkumar
abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

infographic.key_insight: Optimistic reward verifiers can incentivize padding that raises proxy scores while reducing true process faithfulness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Audit verifier selection errors and gap direction, then run a short saturation pilot before trusting reward gains in reinforcement learning.
method: Build executable authorization policies with exact minimal-reason oracles across 124,416 contexts.
Train against seven degraded verifier types while scoring every rollout with the exact oracle.
Test recurring failure patterns across nine configurations spanning frameworks, vendors, and training settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 96 held-out episodes, the sufficiency proxy reached 0.940 while true faithfulness fell from 0.731 to 0.667; sufficiency damage was positive in all 10 replication cells and exceeded two standard errors in seven.
infographic.watch_item: Damage magnitude did not replicate, and findings from exact authorization-policy oracles may not transfer directly to domains without computable ground truth.
infographic.paper_title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle

title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
authors: Arunkumar V, Manoranjan Gandhudi, Gangadharan G. R., Arun Prakash, S. Senthilkumar
abstract: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.

infographic.key_insight: An exact verifier can teach a small language model a successful checking procedure without teaching it to find minimal explanations on unfamiliar policies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Authorization audit explainers need separate checks for sufficiency and minimality, because a valid explanation may still include unnecessary facts.
method: Compute exact minimal sufficient reasons for decisions from executable authorization policies.
Give explainers 30 turns to probe altered requests and test candidate explanations without seeing the policy.
Compare algorithm-taught and frontier-taught fine-tuning, prompting, and exact-reward reinforcement learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: A 4B model trained on 2,000 deletion-algorithm traces reached 92% exactness on its training policy; on three unseen public policies, its answers were 94% sufficient but only 48% minimal.
infographic.watch_item: Do not assume exact feedback guarantees transferable reasoning: the learned checking schedule failed to generalize, and reinforcement learning did not improve held-out accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier

title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks
authors: Daniel Kua, Yan Song
abstract: Generative data augmentation adds samples from generative models to a classifier's training set. Many influential studies use generators pre-trained on large external datasets, and so mix the value of synthetic data with knowledge transferred through pretraining. We study the case without external data, where each generator learns only from the classifier's own training set, and ask when and why adding generated samples to that training set raises or lowers the classifier's test accuracy. We train classifiers with four backbones on six datasets, two of them medical, adding samples from four generators. We bound the excess risk of a classifier trained with synthetic data, that is, how far its population risk can lie above the minimum risk within its hypothesis class. The bound charges synthetic data for the total variation distance between the real and generated distributions and credits synthetic data for a larger training set. The gain from adding synthetic data, the fall in population risk, is at most the excess risk of the real-only classifier, which trains on the real images alone. Read through the bound, the experiments suggest that synthetic data help most when our classifiers detect only a small discrepancy between the generated and real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve, and that synthetic data help little or hurt when the detected discrepancy is large. Generators with a larger lower bound on the total variation distance, a bound that we estimate from our own classifiers, tend to help less on five of the six datasets, and on the CIFAR datasets the most accurate backbone gains the least. The bound gives these directions but not the size of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also reaches at the same number of optimizer steps.

infographic.key_insight: Without external pretraining data, synthetic augmentation helps most when generated samples closely match real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate generator–data mismatch and compare against traditional augmentation at matched optimizer steps before investing in synthetic training samples.
method: Train generators only on the classifier’s own training set.
Evaluate four classifier backbones and four generators across six datasets.
Bound excess risk by balancing distribution mismatch against increased training-set size.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six datasets, including two medical datasets, larger estimated lower bounds on total variation distance were associated with less benefit on five datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The risk bound does not explain the magnitude of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also achieves at matched optimizer steps.
infographic.paper_title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks

title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers
authors: Roksana Goworek, Alexander Hickey, Federico Nanni, Martin O'Reilly
abstract: Researchers at MIT recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM), can write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply, and can read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. In a three-day sprint, we replicated and extended these results. Our four findings: (1) Writing weights reproduces. Astra's networks for the game Breakout scored 514, 550 and 307 (versus MIT's 517), and scored just as well on two modified versions of Breakout. Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but often runs out of output tokens. (2) What is new is translating programs into weights. Earlier models could write a good policy as code a generation before they could write network weights, and the networks the models write behave like compiled programs: two models independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python matching its actions in all tested states. On classifying handwritten digits, Astra's networks scored 50% on average, below a simple classifier (82%). (3) Reading weights is mostly reading the input layer. Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly, but on three new games we designed and trained ourselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board, while mostly missing how the game works. (4) Auditing from weights alone is possible but shallow. Without executing code, Astra picked out a small language model poisoned during training in 10 of 10 runs, one poisoned by extra training afterwards in 7 of 10, and a malicious adapter in 23 of 32 cases, but never identified the trigger or malicious behaviour. Open-weight models lag behind. From this early study, we conclude that LLMs can read and write small networks, but that this currently amounts to compiling hand-designed programs and reading the layout of the input layer. It is a promising but early tool for interpretability.

infographic.key_insight: Frontier LLMs can write and inspect small neural networks, but these abilities largely reflect compiling hand-designed programs into weights and recognizing input-layer layouts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Direct weight generation and inspection could support small-network prototyping and preliminary security screening, but do not yet provide deep behavioral interpretation.
method: Replicated direct weight generation for Breakout and tested modified games and handwritten-digit classification.
Decompiled generated networks into Python and tested action agreement.
Evaluated game identification from weights and screening of poisoned models and malicious adapters.
infographic.evidence_signal: Generated Breakout networks scored 514, 550 and 307 versus the prior report’s 517; digit accuracy averaged 50% versus an 82% baseline, while malicious-adapter detection succeeded in 23 of 32 cases.
infographic.watch_item: This three-day study examined small networks; weight-only auditing detected some compromised models but never identified their triggers or malicious behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers

title: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space
authors: Jacky Kumar
abstract: In particle physics, discrepancies between experimental measurements and Standard Model (SM) predictions are commonly interpreted within new theoretical models. In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many operators can contribute simultaneously to different observables, their effects are correlated, and distinct operator combinations can provide comparably good descriptions of the data. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than $1.5σ$. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.

infographic.key_insight: Reinforcement learning can navigate SMEFT operator combinations to discover diverse new-physics hypotheses that improve agreement with experimental data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A compact actor-critic agent offers a strategy for exploring large combinatorial scientific model spaces with correlated effects.
method: Formulate SMEFT operator exploration as sequential decision-making.
Use a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters.
Seek diverse, high-quality multi-operator theories rather than one best-fit theory.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covers 132 particle-physics observables, including 24 deviations above 1.5σ, and compares RL with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify search speedups or establish generalization beyond the tested phenomenological environment.
infographic.paper_title: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space

title: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next
authors: Javier Aguilar Martín
abstract: A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.

infographic.key_insight: Embedding-map distance alone is not a reliable guide to plausible, future-relevant LLM ideas: far-off targets resist text generation, and sparse regions poorly predict subsequent growth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Ideation systems should not use embedding distance or sparsity as standalone objectives for novelty or research promise.
method: Tested whether LLM-generated text can reach random far points and interior gaps in embedding space.
Evaluated whether past-map gap scores predict later growth in Steam, arXiv and patent datasets.
Compared LLM continuations with real follow-ups and tested critique, directional feedback and distance-graded inspiration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Neighbour-free search reached interior gaps at median cosine similarities of 0.57 and 0.47 but far points at only 0.07 and 0.06; gap-score growth forecasts yielded AUCs of 0.30–0.66.
infographic.watch_item: Original tests were registered before execution, but follow-ups came after the main results, and all registration dates rely only on local git commits.
infographic.paper_title: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next

title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
authors: Paul-Andrei Sava, Alexander Küchler, Daniel Kowatsch, Bernhard Grill, Jennifer Pullman, Yanick Fratantonio
abstract: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.

infographic.key_insight: Under a fixed static-analysis budget, model choice determines the trade-off between clearing benign binaries, flagging malware, and escalating uncertain cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLM-assisted malware triage should be configured around acceptable miss rates and analyst escalation capacity, not a single accuracy score.
method: Build a code property graph from each decompiled binary and select seed functions with an LLM-free heuristic.
Let an LLM agent expand the evidence dossier under a fixed inspection budget.
Generate a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict and a behavioral report.
infographic.evidence_signal: Eight models were evaluated on 1,000 Windows PE binaries with a 600-sample test split; after inspecting about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the top model achieved 0.805 strict balanced accuracy and 0.855 triage balanced accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Triage balanced accuracy credits escalated malware, so deployment decisions must also account for escalation workload and the cost of deeper analysis.
infographic.paper_title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models

title: Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion for Decomposable Generative Models
authors: Yucheng Xie, Fu Feng, Jing Wang, Xin Geng, Yong Rui
abstract: Generative model pre-training typically optimizes a model as a whole without explicitly organizing its parameters for selective reuse. Decomposable pre-training instead learns reusable components for downstream adaptation while retaining strong generative performance. However, existing knowledge diversion methods incur substantial parameter overhead through weight factorization and rely on fixed component assignments to induce specialization, potentially compromising in-distribution generation quality. We therefore propose Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion (SGKDiv), which learns how generative knowledge is shared and specialized for effective generation and selective downstream reuse. SGKDiv constructs Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels, preserving native computational structure without SVD-based reparameterization. Calibrated condition-wise routing combines a shared usage prior with conditional adjustments, while complementary regularization shapes their allocation, diversity, and magnitude. Together, these designs replace predefined component assignments with adaptively learned and explicitly regulated knowledge specialization. Experiments across diverse model and training settings demonstrate better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines, alongside stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.

infographic.key_insight: SGKDiv learns shared and specialized knowledge components within generative models, enabling selective downstream reuse while preserving generation quality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables modular adaptation without SVD-based weight factorization, addressing parameter overhead associated with existing knowledge-diversion methods.
method: Build Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels while preserving native computational structure.
Route knowledge using a shared usage prior plus calibrated condition-specific adjustments.
Regularize allocation, diversity, and magnitude to learn specialization rather than impose fixed assignments.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines across diverse settings, and stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify performance gains or routing and regularization overhead, leaving deployment trade-offs unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion for Decomposable Generative Models

title: Optimal Quantum Sensing Algorithms for Discrete-Frequency Spectroscopy
authors: Yu-Jie Liu, Richard R. Allen, Ruohan Shen, Bingtian Ye, Timothy T. Chang, Joonhee Choi
abstract: Spectroscopy is a versatile tool that drives scientific discovery and underpins modern technologies. Quantum sensing offers promising opportunities to advance spectroscopy through enhanced sensitivity and spectral and spatial resolution. However, existing approaches largely focus on improving general measurement capabilities, often overlooking the structure of specific sensing tasks and leaving potential performance gains untapped. Here, we develop an algorithmic approach to quantum sensing tailored to various spectroscopic tasks, providing new avenues for improvement. Specifically, we consider general time-varying signals supported on a known set of $N$ candidate frequencies, a setting we call discrete-frequency spectroscopy. We formulate three types of practically motivated sensing tasks---Detection, Search, and Learning---that require progressively more spectral information. For all tasks, we design optimal quantum sensing algorithms achieving a $\sqrt{N}$ speedup over conventional frequency-scanning approaches. Optimal Detection and Search need only a single-qubit sensor under $π$-pulse control, whereas optimal Learning provably requires coherent processing with a quantum computer. End-to-end numerical simulations incorporating various experimental imperfections predict up to two-orders-of-magnitude speedup in Detection. As an example, we analyze the feasibility of our Detection and Search algorithms for real-world molecular screening based on state-of-the-art nitrogen-vacancy centers. We also show how quantum-computing-enhanced Learning enables wireless communication in a weak-signal regime where conventional methods fail. Our results establish a practical route toward realizing quantum advantages via designing task-specific sensing algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: Task-specific quantum sensing algorithms achieve an optimal √N speedup over conventional frequency scanning for detection, search, and learning across N known candidate frequencies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could accelerate molecular screening with nitrogen-vacancy sensors and enable wireless communication in weak-signal regimes.
method: Model time-varying signals supported on a known set of N candidate frequencies.
Tailor optimal algorithms to Detection, Search, and Learning tasks.
Use a single qubit with π-pulse control for Detection and Search; use coherent quantum-computer processing for optimal Learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: End-to-end numerical simulations incorporating experimental imperfections predict up to two orders of magnitude speedup in Detection, alongside feasibility analyses for nitrogen-vacancy molecular screening.
infographic.watch_item: The reported Detection gains are simulation-based, and optimal Learning requires coherent quantum-computer processing beyond a single-qubit sensor.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal Quantum Sensing Algorithms for Discrete-Frequency Spectroscopy

title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications
authors: Shuyi Ouyang, Xiaojun Tang, Zijian Zou, Xintong Zhang, Mingli Song, Guannan Zhang
abstract: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.

infographic.key_insight: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 separates requirement fulfillment from artifact quality to evaluate AI authoring across multiple visual media.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark helps engineers distinguish compliance with task specifications from the quality of artifacts produced by AI authoring workflows.
method: Define 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces.
Score Task Fulfillment separately from Artifact Performance across Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery.
Use task-specific rating anchors grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across nine model-harness configurations evaluated on all 211 tasks, overall scores ranged from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the highest-to-lowest score gap.
infographic.watch_item: Results characterize model-harness configurations, so score differences should not be attributed to models alone.
infographic.paper_title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications

title: ONAM: Fitting Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for Post-Hoc Interpretability of Black-Box Predictions
authors: David Köhler, Matthias Schmid
abstract: Modern machine learning models, such as artificial neural networks, achieve high predictive performance through increasingly complex black-box architectures, limiting their use in settings where transparency, interpretability, and fairness are required. Here we present the R package ONAM, which provides a novel and practical implementation of functional decomposition, a technique to facilitate the interpretability of black-box models through structured effect representations. ONAM implements an algorithmic framework for the post-hoc decomposition of predictions into components associated with different input features. The package is designed for usability and efficiency, including functionalities for visualization as well as quantitative measures to assess interpretability. As a model-agnostic method, it can be applied to a wide range of prediction models. We describe the mathematical foundations, algorithmic design, and software architecture of ONAM. A central result of the proposed methodology is that the resulting decomposition satisfies the condition of hierarchical orthogonality, thereby guaranteeing that all components are identifiable and uniquely defined.

infographic.key_insight: ONAM decomposes black-box predictions into structured feature effects with hierarchical orthogonality, making the components identifiable and uniquely defined.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model-agnostic R package supports post-hoc interpretation of prediction models through effect visualizations and quantitative interpretability measures.
method: Apply functional decomposition to black-box predictions.
Fit structured components associated with input features.
Enforce hierarchical orthogonality to identify components uniquely.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports mathematical foundations, algorithmic design, and software architecture, but provides no datasets or quantitative evaluation results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical decomposition fidelity and computational cost should be evaluated for the target model and dataset.
infographic.paper_title: ONAM: Fitting Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for Post-Hoc Interpretability of Black-Box Predictions
